name: Aplos
summary: Fund accounting built for nonprofits and faith-based organisations, tracking restricted and unrestricted money separately. A 50%-off-for-three-months promotion was running again in September 2026, under a new code and to a new date, so check what month four costs.
best_for: small nonprofits and faith-based organisations that need true fund accounting rather than general small-business bookkeeping — tracking restricted and unrestricted funds separately is the thing generic tools genuinely cannot do
skip_if: you are a normal for-profit business, because you are paying for fund accounting you will never use; also skip Lite if several people need access but should not all be able to see and change everything — every Lite user is an Administrator, and role permissions start at Core
honest_knock: The headline you will see first is not the price you will pay. The 50%-off banner sits at the top of the page and rewrites every figure on it, so the $39.50 that catches your eye is a three-month rate against a $79 list price — a 100% increase waiting in month four, on software that holds your books and is therefore painful to leave. The second thing to pin down is what grows with you: each user beyond the two included adds $20 a month, every 1,000 contacts beyond 500 adds another $20, and on Lite every user is a full Administrator, because role permissions start at Core.

pricing.entry_price_terms: Lite · billed monthly, as published for all three tiers
pricing.notes: (2026-10-13, read on their own pricing page and in their help centre) Three published tiers, billed monthly: Lite at $79/month, Core at $129 and Advanced at $229, plus a fourth Custom tier with tailored pricing aimed at organisations above $1 million in annual revenue. Advanced is framed as a quote rather than a checkout: the card reads "Customized solutions start at $229/month" and the button asks for a demo. A promotion was running when we re-read the page on 13 October 2026 — 50% off for three months with code FALL26, showing Lite at $39.50 and Core at $64.50 — and the footnote dates it: new customers only, ending 31 October. On 10 September the same FALL26 offer was dated to 30 September, and in August it ran as SUMMER26 to 31 August, so the deadline moves. What matters is still what you pay in month four. The trial is 15 days and takes no credit card. Lite and Core each include 2 users; Advanced includes 3. Aplos's help centre ('How to Manage Your Subscription', read 13 October 2026) adds what the plan cards leave out: all platform subscriptions include two users and further users cost $20 per month per user; the base subscription includes up to 500 contacts and the price rises $20 a month for each additional 1,000; and annual billing receives a 10% discount.

compare_with.name: QuickBooks
compare_with.why: the comparison every nonprofit treasurer ends up making, and it turns on one question rather than price. QuickBooks is cheaper and more widely known, but it tracks classes, not funds — so restricted and unrestricted money live in the same pot with a label on top. If your auditor or your grant terms require true fund separation, that difference is the whole decision and the price gap is secondary

exit_test.what: On 24 October 2026, in the trial account from this test, we exported our two imported test contacts, then re-imported them with the Contact IDs from the export and one changed address.
exit_test.first_import: Re-importing with the Contact ID column mapped to 'Contact ID' created no duplicates: still three contacts. The unchanged contact kept one address. For the other contact the old address was not replaced: it now had two addresses, the old and the changed one, both marked 'Other' and NOT VERIFIED, and the list still showed the old one as primary. Every column had to be mapped by hand again.
exit_test.awkward: The XLSX has a title row ('Contacts for organization …') above the column headers, and the Contact ID shows in Excel as a number in scientific notation (2.6552421E7).

sessions.what: Tested by our team on 24 October 2026 during the free trial, set up as a fictional non-profit, without a bank or payment connection, donations or a card: Daan created the account and our AI assistant ran the test in Daan's browser. We imported two made-up contacts with addresses, exported them, and re-imported them with their Contact IDs and one changed address.
findings: After upload, every column of our file started as 'DO NOT IMPORT', including obvious ones such as First Name and Email, so each column has to be mapped by hand. Both contacts then came in with their addresses.

Re-importing with the Contact ID mapped created no duplicates, but a changed address did not replace the old one: the contact ended up with both addresses, marked 'Other' and NOT VERIFIED, and the list kept showing the old address as primary.

Export Contacts lets you choose the columns and downloads an XLSX straight away. Both test contacts came back complete with their Contact ID; the file has a title row above the headers, and Excel shows the Contact ID in scientific notation.

No card was asked. A banner offered 25% off for six months when subscribing within the first 15 days; the app did not show a trial end date. The new account already held a contact for Aplos itself, and showed banners for other products of the parent company.
sessions.note: Findings as written up after the session; no pass/fail per task was scored.
